title: Urania: 'The meaning, not the Name I call'
short: The third invocation names the Muse Urania, but in the sense of her name, 'heavenly', not as the classical Muse of astronomy.
body: Urania was the classical Muse of astronomy, and Du Bartas had already made her 'the Christian Muse' in his poems on the creation, as the Dartmouth edition notes. Milton immediately qualifies the name: 'The meaning, not the Name I call'. Verity explains that Urania means 'the Heavenly one', and that Milton invokes a heavenly power, not one of the nine. She was born before the hills and played with 'Eternal Wisdom thy Sister' in God's presence: Verity identifies Proverbs 8:23-30, where Wisdom says 'I was by him ... rejoicing always before him', and notes that the Vulgate's 'ludens' ('playing') underlies Milton's 'didst play', a verse he also quotes in Tetrachordon. The halfway invocation marks the turn from war in Heaven to creation, and from the classical to the biblical.

title: Bellerophon ... th' Aleian Field
greek: Greek Bellerophontês; Alêïon pedion, 'plain of wandering'
short: The poet fears falling like Bellerophon, who tried to ride Pegasus to heaven, was thrown, and wandered blind and alone on the Aleian plain.
body: Having soared 'Above th' Olympian Hill', the poet asks to be brought safely down, lest 'from this flying Steed unrein'd, (as once Bellerophon, though from a lower Clime) Dismounted, on th' Aleian Field I fall Erroneous there to wander and forlorne'. Verity explains the legend: Bellerophon tried to ride the winged horse Pegasus up to the gods and was thrown; hated by the gods, he wandered alone in the Aleian plain, whose name suggests 'wandering', as Homer tells (Iliad 6.200-02). 'Erroneous' has its Latin sense, 'straying'. The fear of erring and falling has a pointed edge for a poet who was blind when he wrote it. The image recalls the 'adventrous Song' of 1.13-15 and warns against the overreaching flight the poem condemns in Satan and Eve.

title: though fall'n on evil dayes ... and evil tongues
short: Milton's most direct reference to his own situation after the Restoration: blind, endangered, slandered, and in solitude, yet still singing.
body: 'Standing on Earth', the poet sings 'with mortal voice, unchang'd To hoarce or mute, though fall'n on evil dayes, On evil dayes though fall'n, and evil tongues; In darkness, and with dangers compast round, And solitude'. Verity explains the circumstances: after the Restoration of 1660 Milton, who had defended the execution of Charles I, was arrested and imprisoned for some months and escaped further punishment only through the efforts of friends such as Andrew Marvell; 'darkness' is his blindness and 'evil tongues' the abuse of royalist enemies. The chiastic repetition of the line ('evil dayes ... fall'n, ... fall'n ... evil dayes') expresses, as Verity notes, both pathos and steadiness. The phrase 'unchang'd' answers Satan's 'how chang'd' (1.84): the poet, unlike the fallen angels, has not altered his allegiance.

title: fit audience find, though few
short: The poet asks Urania to find him a fit audience, even if a small one: an echo of Horace that also implies a spiritually and politically select readership.
body: 'Still govern thou my Song, Urania, and fit audience find, though few'. Verity identifies the source in Horace, who is content with few readers (Satires 1.10.74, 'contentus paucis lectoribus'), and notes Wordsworth's quotation of the line in The Recluse. Milton's 'fit' carries more than literary taste: the Dartmouth edition suggests a readership religiously and politically fit, the godly remnant who shared his values in a hostile time. The line has become a motto for writers who value understanding over popularity. Verity's note also corrects any idea that the poem was neglected: it sold steadily and Milton was much visited by admirers after its publication.

title: Bacchus and his Revellers ... that tore the Thracian Bard In Rhodope
short: The poet prays to be protected from the 'barbarous dissonance' that destroyed Orpheus, torn apart by Bacchants while his mother the Muse could not save him.
body: Milton asks Urania to 'drive farr off the barbarous dissonance Of Bacchus and his Revellers, the Race Of that wilde Rout that tore the Thracian Bard In Rhodope'. Orpheus, the legendary Thracian singer whose music moved woods and rocks, was torn to pieces by the frenzied women followers of Bacchus on Mount Rhodope, and his head floated down the Hebrus (Ovid, Metamorphoses 11.1-55; Virgil, Georgics 4.517-27). His mother Calliope, Muse of epic, could not save him: 'So fail not thou, who thee implores: For thou art Heav'nlie, shee an empty dreame'. Verity notes the parallel in Lycidas 58-63 and suggests a comparison between the Bacchic rout and the dissolute Restoration court, with a hint that the poet feared Orpheus' fate. The classical Muse is dismissed as 'an empty dreame'.

title: Knowledge is as food, and needs no less Her Temperance
short: Raphael warns that knowledge, like food, must be taken with temperance; too much 'turns Wisdom to Folly, as Nourishment to Winde'.
body: Raphael agrees to tell Adam how the world was made, but sets bounds: 'Enough is left besides to search and know. But Knowledge is as food, and needs no less Her Temperance over Appetite, to know In measure what the mind may well contain, Oppresses else with Surfet, and soon turns Wisdom to Folly, as Nourishment to Winde'. Verity cross-refers to the same sentiment, 'knowledge within bounds', in 8.173-97. The metaphor is pointed in a poem whose catastrophe is caused by eating forbidden fruit in the hope of knowledge; Eve's fall is literally an appetite for knowledge without temperance. The Dartmouth edition notes Adam's own distinction between seeking God's secrets and seeking knowledge 'the more To magnifie his works' (7.96-97).

title: I am who fill Infinitude ... uncircumscrib'd my self retire
short: God fills all space yet withdraws his goodness from parts of it; in that free withdrawal the world is made. The passage is a famous crux of Milton's theology.
body: The Father tells the Son to create a world: 'Boundless the Deep, because I am who fill Infinitude, nor vacuous the space. Though I uncircumscrib'd my self retire, And put not forth my goodness, which is free To act or not, Necessitie and Chance Approach not mee, and what I will is Fate'. Verity quotes Keightley's paraphrase: Chaos has no limits because the infinite God fills it, though he shows his goodness only where he chooses; compare 'Do not I fill heaven and earth? saith the Lord' (Jeremiah 23:24). Scholars have compared the idea of divine self-withdrawal with the Kabbalistic doctrine of tsimtsum, God's contraction to make room for creation, though whether Milton knew it is disputed. The last line is pointed against the devils' fatalism (2.560; 5.860): there is no Fate above God, only his free will.

title: He took the golden Compasses
short: The Son marks out the bounds of the universe in Chaos with golden compasses, an image from Proverbs 8:27 and Dante later painted by Blake.
body: Riding out in the Father's chariot to the edge of Chaos, the Son 'took the golden Compasses, prepar'd In Gods Eternal store, to circumscribe This Universe, and all created things: One foot he center'd, and the other turn'd Round through the vast profunditie obscure, And said, thus farr extend, thus farr thy bounds'. Verity traces the image to Proverbs 8:27, where Wisdom says 'When he prepared the heavens, I was there: when he set a compass upon the face of the depth', and to Dante, where God is 'He who turned the compass round the limit of the world' (Paradiso 19.40-42). The Dartmouth edition notes Blake's design The Ancient of Days. Creation, in Milton, is the setting of bounds and order on the boundless, followed by the Spirit's brooding 'on the watrie calme' (7.235).

title: Let ther be Light ... Ethereal, first of things, quintessence pure
short: Light, created on the first day before the sun, is 'Ethereal, first of things', a fifth element purer than the four; the sun only later becomes its tabernacle.
body: Raphael repeats God's words in Genesis 1:3, 'Let ther be Light', and calls the new light 'Ethereal, first of things, quintessence pure'. Verity explains that ether, the 'fifth essence' (quintessence) of Aristotelian physics, was thought to be the pure substance of the heavens, distinct from the four elements, and links the line with the invocation 'Hail holy Light, ofspring of Heav'n first-born' (3.1). Because Genesis creates light on the first day and the sun only on the fourth (Genesis 1:14-18), Milton, as Verity notes, held that light exists independently of the sun, which later becomes its 'Tabernacle' (Psalm 19:4; 7.248). The angels hail the first evening and morning with song, as in Job 38:7, 'when the morning stars sang together'.

title: the Pleiades before him danc'd Shedding sweet influence
short: On the first morning the sun rises with the Pleiades, the spring constellation, whose 'sweet influence' comes from Job 38:31.
body: The newly made sun rises, 'jocond to run His Longitude through Heav'ns high rode', and 'the gray Dawn, and the Pleiades before him danc'd Shedding sweet influence'. Verity identifies the source: 'Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?' (Job 38:31), and explains that the Pleiades, the seven-star cluster (in legend the daughters of Atlas, as the Dartmouth edition notes), rise with the sun near the spring equinox; a common belief held that the world was created in spring, and that before the Fall spring was perpetual (4.268; 10.679). 'Influence' is a technical term of astrology, the ethereal fluid believed to flow from the stars and affect earthly things. The sun's running 'as a strong man to run a race' is Psalm 19:5.

title: Leviathan Hugest of living Creatures
short: The whale created on the fifth day sleeps 'like a Promontorie' or swims 'a moving Land', recalling the sinister Leviathan simile for Satan in Book I.
body: Among the sea creatures of the fifth day 'Leviathan Hugest of living Creatures, on the Deep Stretcht like a Promontorie sleeps or swimmes, And seems a moving Land, and at his Gilles Draws in, and at his Trunck spouts out a Sea'. Verity identifies Leviathan here as the whale and refers back to the simile of 1.200-08, where Satan is compared to the same creature mistaken for an island; the Dartmouth edition makes the same connection. The repetition is instructive: in its proper place in creation the great beast is simply a wonder of God's making, while in Hell it served as an image of deceptive power. Milton's monsters are good in themselves; evil lies in perversion and misuse. The source is Job 41 and Psalm 104:26, 'there is that leviathan, whom thou hast made to play therein'.

title: The Tawnie Lion, pawing to get free ... Behemoth biggest born of Earth
short: On the sixth day the beasts struggle out of the soil half-formed, the lion pawing to free his hinder parts and Behemoth, the elephant, heaving up his bulk.
body: The earth gives birth to the animals in a vivid sequence: 'The grassie Clods now Calv'd, now half appeer'd The Tawnie Lion, pawing to get free His hinder parts, then springs as broke from Bonds'; the ounce, the 'Libbard' (leopard) and the tiger rise 'as the Moale' upheaves the soil, and 'Behemoth biggest born of Earth upheav'd His vastness'. Verity glosses Behemoth as the elephant (the beast of Job 40:15, 'Behold now behemoth, which I made with thee'), 'libbard' as the old form of leopard, and the 'river-horse' as the hippopotamus. The idea of animals born from the earth echoes classical accounts of spontaneous generation, such as Ovid's creatures emerging from the mud after the flood (Metamorphoses 1.416-37). Readers have long admired the half-comic energy of the half-formed lion.

title: The Parsimonious Emmet ... in her popular Tribes Of Commonaltie
short: The thrifty ant, a pattern of 'just equalitie' in a commonwealth, and the bees with their 'Female' workers: political natural history, which Verity calls Milton's republicanism.
body: The ant ('Emmet') is 'Parsimonious', 'provident Of future, in small room large heart enclos'd, Pattern of just equalitie perhaps Hereafter, join'd in her popular Tribes Of Commonaltie'. Verity notes Horace's ant, 'not ignorant or careless of the future' (Satires 1.1.35), and Virgil's bees with great spirits in small breasts (Georgics 4.83), and comments simply that here 'Milton shows his republicanism'. Proverbs 6:6-8 had already made the ant a moral example: 'Go to the ant, thou sluggard'. The bees that follow, who 'feed Thir Husband Drone' and build waxen cells, reflect the belief, which Verity notes, that worker bees were female and drones male. In Milton's day the bee hive was a common image of monarchy; the ant colony offered a republican alternative.

title: in his own Image hee Created thee ... Male he created thee, but thy consort Female
short: Man is made upright, rational and in God's image to rule the other creatures; Raphael's wording combines the two Genesis accounts of the creation of man and woman.
body: The sixth day culminates in 'a Creature who not prone And Brute as other Creatures, but endu'd With Sanctitie of Reason, might erect His Stature'. Verity notes that Milton treats upright posture as a sign of superiority and that he recalls Ovid's creation of man, who alone looks up to heaven (Metamorphoses 1.76-86). God says 'Let us make now Man in our image', which the Dartmouth edition notes Milton resolves by having the Father address the Son. 'In his own Image hee Created thee, in the Image of God Express' echoes Genesis 1:27 and, as Verity observes, Hebrews 1:3 ('express image'). 'Male he created thee, but thy consort Female for Race' blends Genesis 1, where male and female are made together, with Genesis 2, where Eve is made later from Adam's rib, a combination critics such as Mary Nyquist have analysed.

title: the Galaxie, that Milkie way ... powderd with Starrs
short: The Son returns to Heaven along the Milky Way, pictured as the road to God's house, 'powderd with Starrs'.
body: The Son ascends after six days' work along 'a broad And ample rode, whose dust is Gold And pavement Starrs, as Starrs to thee appeer, Seen in the Galaxie, that Milkie way'. 'Galaxy' comes from Greek gala, 'milk', and Milton glosses the Greek word with the English, as Newton observed (cited by Verity on 7.619). Verity also notes Milton's Latin phrase for the Milky Way in an early elegy and Burton's description of it as 'a confused light of small Stars'. The idea of the Milky Way as the road of the gods to Jupiter's palace comes from Ovid (Metamorphoses 1.168-71). The phrase 'as Starrs to thee appeer' reminds Adam, and the reader, that the description is accommodated to human sight.

title: With Halleluiahs: Thus was Sabbath kept
short: The seventh day is kept in Heaven with music and praise; the angels' hymn calls the world-makers' work greater than the defeat of the rebels.
body: On the seventh day God rests 'from work, but not in silence holy kept': harps, pipes, dulcimers and organs sound, incense rises, and the angels sing the creation. Verity glosses the instruments (the dulcimer of Daniel 3:5) and Hallelujah, 'praise ye the Lord'. Their song makes a bold point: 'to create Is greater then created to destroy' (7.606-07), so the making of the world outshines the victory over the 'Giant Angels', whom Verity compares with the Giants of classical myth. The hymn ends with a blessing on mankind modelled on Virgil's 'O fortunatos nimium, sua si bona norint' (Georgics 2.458), as Verity notes: 'thrice happie if they know Thir happiness, and persevere upright'. The conditional 'if' casts its shadow over the rest of the poem.
